paras: The killing of Joe Sanders was the shooting of a Black man by a posse of citizens at Henderson, Texas, on August 22, 1903. Sanders had been accused of attempting a criminal assault on a young girl the night before, and the men who came to arrest him shot him to death at his door. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and the Cleveland Gazette reprinted it without comment.

According to the dispatch, Sanders was accused of having attempted a criminal assault on a young girl on the night of August 21; the Louisville Courier-Journal's copy described her as a "young white girl." The next day a group described as "a posse of citizens" went to his house to arrest him. When the men approached, Sanders was standing in his door holding a shotgun, and he was "struck by four loads of buckshot" and killed. No copy names any member of the posse or any officer, and none says that Sanders fired.
No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury action concerning the posse appears in the coverage, which consists entirely of the single dispatch and its condensations.

The dispatch appeared on August 23 in papers from St. Paul and Salt Lake City to Birmingham, Raleigh, Savannah, Richmond and Louisville, and condensed versions ran in weekly digests into early September. Southern headlines treated the accusation as proven: the Birmingham Age-Herald ran "Negro Rapist Shot," the Savannah Morning News "Would-Be Rapist Shot to Death" over "Texas Posse Gives Short Shift to a Black Fiend," and the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger "Assaulter Killed." The Courier-Journal's subhead said Sanders "Resisted Efforts To Arrest Him," while the Atlanta Constitution headed the same text "Shot to Death by Texas Mob."

Northern papers more often built their headlines on the shotgun, as in the St. Paul Globe's "Faces the Citizens With a Shotgun," which added that Sanders was "Summarily Shot to Death," and the Daily Pioneer's "Posse Shoots First." The Richmond Times Dispatch printed the dispatch under a Henderson, Kentucky, dateline, and the Clinton Caucasian dated the accusation to "Saturday night" and the shooting to "Sunday." The only Black-press report found, in the Cleveland Gazette of August 29, repeated the wire account in a digest of national news without headline or comment.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Henderson
accounts.gist: Sanders, accused of attempting criminal assault on a young girl the night before, was standing in his door holding a shotgun when citizens came to arrest him, and was shot to death with four loads of buckshot.

accounts.label: Black press digest
accounts.gist: The Cleveland Gazette repeated the wire version, including the shotgun in the door, without comment.

framing.detail: Southern papers headed the dispatch 'Negro Rapist Shot', 'Would-Be Rapist Shot to Death', 'Texas Posse Gives Short Shift to a Black Fiend' and 'Assaulter Killed', treating the accusation as proven.
Northern and western papers ran the dispatch under neutral or shotgun-centered headlines ('Faces the Citizens With a Shotgun', 'Posse Shoots First'), or as one-line digest items.
The Atlanta Constitution headed the same text 'Shot to Death by Texas Mob', while the Courier-Journal's subhead said Sanders 'Resisted Efforts To Arrest Him'.
The Cleveland Gazette carried the wire sentences in its unheaded news digest, between unrelated items, without comment.

conflicts.note: The Richmond Times Dispatch printed the same AP text under a Kentucky dateline; every other copy says Texas, and the St. Paul headline calls Sanders 'a Texas Negro', so the Kentucky dateline is an error.

versions.value: Accused 'last night', shot 'to-day', dispatch dated Aug. 22

conflicts.note: The Aug. 22 dateline appears in the fullest and earliest copies, which ran on Aug. 23; the weekday version and the Aug. 25 dateline appear only in later rewrites.
Only the Courier-Journal's copy names the girl's race.
